stories.title: Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5MRuX Uber has become part of daily life for people across the world, like here in Australia. But financial shrotcomings have forced the ride-hailing app to shrink its footprint in Africa Image: Xinhua/picture alliance Advertisement A week ago, Uber unexpectedly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending more than a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also said it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect. With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda , Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa. "This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition," without sharing details on what this assistance would entail. In the last year, the multinational company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania, while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.

Annoncé par le gouvernement il y a une dizaine d'années comme un projet phare d'infrastructure sportive, parmi ceux qui étaient destinés à accueillir les matchs de la Coupe d'Afrique des nations qui s'est jouée dans le pays entre janvier et février 2022, le chantier pour l'achèvement des travaux du complexe est à l'arrêt. Au quartier Olembé, dans la périphérie ouest de la capitale Yaoundé, un écrin de 60 000 places est bien sorti de terre, mais les travaux d'embellissement et plusieurs structures annexes restent inachevés. Le complexe d'Olembé fait aussi désormais l'objet de plusieurs procédures contentieuses entre l'État et les différents constructeurs qui se sont succédé sur le chantier. Il en est ainsi du groupe italien Piccini, qui a obtenu le 4 septembre d'un tribunal arbitral, le Cirdi, basé à New York aux États-Unis, une sentence en sa faveur pour un dédommagement de 51 milliards de francs CFA.

Those being extradited were arrested in 2021 and are believed to be members of crime syndicate Black Axe - a Nigerian mafia-style gang tied to human trafficking, internet fraud and murder. The bombshell decision was announced by Norwegian Foreign Affairs Minister Espen Barth Eide, who blamed mounting global instability and what he chillingly described as the most serious security policy situation the world has faced since the Second World War. The closure will bring the curtain down on 27 years of diplomatic presence in the country. The embassy, first established in 2000, has been a cornerstone of Norway's development partnership with Malawi, pumping in roughly NOK500 million -- around K93 billion -- in assistance every year in recent times. That support has poured into critical sectors including health, education, agriculture and good governance, making Norway one of Malawi's most significant development partners.

The vessel was first noticed around South Beach late Wednesday night. Residents secured it hours later with ropes before Coast Guard personnel, the Liberia National Police and other security agencies took over the scene and towed it to the base on Bushrod Island for examination. Although Uganda is a republic, it contains several ancient kingdoms whose leaders are still held in high regard as keepers of tradition and maintain significant social influence. Oyo, who was also known by his regnal name Rukidi IV, became the world's youngest monarch at the age of three in 1995 following the death of his father. King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who ruled the Tooro Kingdom for more than three decades, was undergoing cancer treatment in the US when he died last month aged 34 . Royal clan elders have named popular TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56, as the next monarch, but this has been rejected by Oyo's close family. His sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said the late king had left a will written in 2022 naming his young son, whose identity has never been disclosed, as his successor. stories.title: Russia to open more cultural centres in Africa as it seeks to broaden influence

The centres will promote the Russian language, education, science and culture, while supporting various projects, Russia's humanitarian agency says. Known as "Russian Houses", eight of 11 new centres are due to open in Africa, where 16 have already been set up over the years. Russia's state-controlled paramilitary force African Corps, which replaced the Wagner Group's mercenary operations, has become a key security partner for multiple military governments in the West Africa in the fight against jihadist insurgencies. In particular the juntas in Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso turned to the Russian mercenaries, now Africa Corps, as they sought to shrug off influence from their former colonial power France.

stories.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JTSL Unai Eizaguirre, an eel fisherman for 30 years, prepares gear with a colleague in the Basque Country Image: Nicole Ris/DW Advertisement In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades. The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species , which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels. "So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre, who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous." Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed. "The situation is so bad that we have to act on everything," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI.

stories.title: 'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Police used tear gas to disperse hundreds of protesters who took to the streets on Monday over prolonged power cuts By Wycliffe Muia Â and Â Thomas Naadi Published 9 September 2026 The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa. His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours. "When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month. The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal. The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand. stories.title: ‘This is what I have to do to survive’: the Sudan refugees forced into sex work
stories.summary: Illustration: Patrycja Podkościelny for The Guardian View image in fullscreen Illustration: Patrycja Podkościelny for The Guardian ‘This is what I have to do to survive’: the Sudan refugees forced into sex work They fled a brutal civil war to reach safety in Egypt, but now many Sudanese women and girls are falling prey to sexual exploitation S udanese women who fled to Egypt to escape the war in their country are facing increasing levels of sexual exploitation, with the Guardian told of single mothers forced to sell their bodies to survive and feed their children. Many of the women have not previously worked in Sudan , where conservative social norms dictate that men are usually responsible for financial support. Without established trades or professions, and with their husbands and other family members dead or missing, many female refugees are struggling to pay for food, medical care and rent. The Guardian spoke to 19 aid workers, refugees and medical professionals who say a lack of access to healthcare, education and, at times, food has made the situation for Sudanese women in Egypt increasingly desperate. Sudan’s civil war triggered the world’s worst displacement crisis, forcing more than 4.5 million people to flee to neighbouring Chad, South Sudan, Libya and Egypt.

stories.title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
stories.summary: Image caption, David Etor's first break came after designing and building a kind of "solar oven" in Nigeria By James Diamond ,Â Bristol Â and Â John Darvall ,Â BBC Radio Bristol Published 7 September 2026 A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field. David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in the School of Electrical, Electronic and Mechanical Engineering at the University of Bristol. He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our dignity" in front of neighbours. "I didn't see a way out," he said. 'The poor called us poor' Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his memoir, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom. "It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said. "I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water. "[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food... "She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water. "She was trying to protect our dignity." stories.title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
stories.summary: Image caption, The Mercator projection is the map widely used across the globe but inaccurately depicts the sizes of countries and continents By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 5 September 2026 Updated 6 September 2026 The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents such as Africa. The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy with the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger. The UN adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own. There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks. Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday. The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime. The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.
